<reason>Side B's opening reframe (resident priority as reallocation inside a conservation-set cap) was a genuinely good move that killed A's "one more body" attack, and B's honest concession in A1 plus the closing distinction between compensation (levy) and access (priority) gave it a real live route. But A converted that concession into the decisive weighing question — "what does the exclusion buy?" — and B never fully repaired two resulting holes: (1) the yield problem, since a discounted resident slot inside a fixed cap is a forgone full-price slot, and B's dynamic-pricing escape was plausibly shown to be A's own levy doing the work; and (2) B's own 10–20% quota number, which A turned into "four in five residents still shut out, identically, while the restoration budget shrinks." B's second rebuttal and closing largely restated the stewardship-claim frame and dropped the revenue clash entirely. A also handled B's pressure questions cleanly (neutral scarcity vs. categorical exclusion; exclusion that funds the fabric vs. exclusion that funds a postcode) and kept narrowing rather than widening. Both sides used ordinary knowledge and plausible mechanisms without fake sourcing; both used correct A1:/A2: structure. A's rhetoric ("It is a raffle"; "let nobody's exclusion be for nothing") was tied to real argumentative work rather than decoration.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's exploitation of B's answers: taking B's admitted "no physical effect" plus B's own 10–20% quota figure and combining them into "the site loses peak revenue, the once-in-a-lifetime visitor loses the cathedral, and four in five residents are still excluded — the exclusion buys nothing." B's best counter (money is compensation, not access) landed but never answered the revenue-yield or minority-benefit half of that package.</best_rebuttal>
